core: A grid is a framework of intersecting lines that structures where elements sit on a page and creates consistent relationships between them
The anatomy of a grid: format, margins, columns, rows, gutters, modules, flowlines, spatial zones (regions), and markers
The main grid types: manuscript/block, column, modular, and hierarchical grids
The baseline grid: evenly spaced horizontal lines that anchor text to a shared vertical rhythm
The historical roots of the modern typographic grid in the Swiss / International Typographic Style, attributed to Josef Muller-Brockmann and his 1981 book Grid Systems in Graphic Design
Modern responsive web grids, e.g. the 12-column grid with a container, columns, and gutters that reflows across breakpoints
Why grids create order, alignment, efficiency, and consistency, and that a grid is a tool that can be broken deliberately

claims.claim: A grid is a network of intersecting vertical and horizontal lines that structures the placement of elements and creates relationships between them, dividing the design space into sections and acting as a bridge between a design concept and its implementation.

The parts of a grid include the format (the whole area, e.g. the page or browser window), margins (the negative space between the format edge and the content), columns (vertical bands), rows (horizontal bands), gutters (the spaces separating columns and rows), modules (individual units of space at regular intervals), flowlines (horizontal lines that break the space into bands and create alignment points), spatial zones (fields of adjacent modules assigned a function), and markers (placement indicators for repeating items such as page numbers/folios).

The four commonly taught grid types are the manuscript grid (a single large block for continuous text, as in a book), the column grid (multiple vertical columns separated by gutters, good for discontinuous information), the modular grid (a column grid subdivided by horizontal lines into a matrix of equal modules, good for complex/tabular content), and the hierarchical grid (irregular, content-driven divisions used when the regular grids do not fit).

A baseline grid is a set of evenly spaced horizontal lines that determines where all the type will sit, anchoring text and other elements to a common leading (line spacing) so they align across columns and pages and produce a consistent vertical rhythm.

A common proportioning convention sets the gutter between columns at a width x and the outer margins at roughly 2x, so that when margins are wider than the gutters the eye is guided inward toward the content.

The modern typographic grid grew out of the post-war Swiss / International Typographic Style; Josef Muller-Brockmann (1914-1996) systematized it through his Tonhalle Zurich concert posters (produced c. 1951-1972) and his 1981 bilingual textbook Grid Systems in Graphic Design (Verlag Arthur Niggli), which remains in print and widely assigned.

Muller-Brockmann held that graphic design achieves objectivity through systematic construction rather than personal expression, and that the grid is an aid, not a guarantee: one must learn to use it, which requires practice.

Modern responsive web layouts commonly use a 12-column grid: columns live inside a container (fixed or full width) and are separated by gutters, and the grid reflows across responsive breakpoints so that columns which sit side by side on wide screens stack vertically on narrow ones (mobile-first). In Bootstrap 5 the default is 12 columns with a 1.5rem gutter and six breakpoints.

Consistent margins and columns create an underlying structure that unifies multiple pages of a document or website and makes the layout process more efficient; the plan for the grid should come from the content and concept of the project.

Dividing a content width W into n equal columns separated by (n-1) gutters of width g gives a column width of (W - (n-1)*g)/n; e.g. a 190 mm content width in 3 columns with 5 mm gutters yields 60 mm columns, and a 1200 px container in 12 columns with 24 px gutters yields 78 px columns.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many 'types' of grid there are and what to call them.
positions: Timothy Samara's widely used taxonomy names four: manuscript, column, modular, and hierarchical (baseline treated as a component that underlies the others).
Some OER and practitioner texts organize grids as single-column, multi-column, modular, and baseline, treating the baseline grid as its own type.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the four-type Samara taxonomy (manuscript, column, modular, hierarchical) as the primary framing and presents the baseline grid separately as the horizontal rhythm that underlies text-heavy layouts, noting that different texts slice the categories slightly differently.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the golden ratio is a reliable basis for grid proportions.
positions: Some design texts present the golden section (1:1.618) as a time-tested proportioning tool for page and column layout.
The subject source-map cautions that claims the golden ratio explains great design are frequently overstated.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson mentions the golden ratio only as one of several proportioning conventions a designer may use to set margins/columns, and does not assert it explains or guarantees good design.

sourceRecords.title: Anatomy of a Modular Typographic Grid
sourceRecords.notes: Practitioner reference, read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports the definitions of the parts of a grid: format (the whole area — page or browser window), margins (negative space between the format edge and the content), flowlines (horizontal lines that break the space into bands and create alignment points), modules (individual units of space at regular intervals; width from text measure, height from leading), spatial zones (fields of adjacent modules, each with a designated function), columns (vertical bands of modules), rows (horizontal bands), gutters (the spaces separating modules, recommended minimum ~1em), and markers (placement indicators for repeating items such as folios/page numbers). Treated as REFERENCE_ONLY per subject source-map; facts synthesized, no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: 4 Types of Grids And When Each Works Best
sourceRecords.notes: Practitioner reference, read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Supports the four-type taxonomy: manuscript grid (a single large block for extensive continuous text, e.g. books/essays), column grid (multiple vertical columns separated by gutters, good for discontinuous information — text, images, captions in different columns), modular grid (a column grid with added horizontal divisions forming a matrix of cells/modules, good for complex and tabular content, with adjacent modules combining into spatial zones), and hierarchical grid (organic, content-driven proportions used when the other grids do not fit). Also supports the convention that gutters are sized at 'x' with margins at '2x' so the eye is guided inward, and that flowlines/baselines position elements vertically. This four-type framing derives from Timothy Samara's Making and Breaking the Grid. REFERENCE_ONLY; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Grid system — Bootstrap v5.0 Documentation
sourceRecords.notes: Official documentation of a widely used responsive CSS framework, read via WebFetch 2026-08-19. Used to describe the generic modern responsive column grid: a 12-column template per row, columns placed inside a container (fixed .container or full-width .container-fluid), gutters implemented as column padding (Bootstrap 5 default gutter 1.5rem) with negative row margins, six responsive breakpoints using min-width media queries, and mobile-first stacking (columns stack vertically on the smallest screens and sit side by side on wider ones). Used for the concept, not framework-specific syntax; no proprietary assets reproduced.

Cross-checked against general design-history knowledge and the BCcampus OER's mention of the International Typographic Style. REFERENCE_ONLY; facts synthesized, no wording reproduced.
